speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
maintopic: SUDETEN IMMIGRANTS
subtopic: SETTLEMENT IN CANADA OP FAMILIES FROM CZECHO-SLOVAKIA
speechtext:
A few days ago questions were asked in regard to the matter of the proposed settlement in Canada of some Sudeten German refugees. I may say at once that there has been some misunderstanding as to the actual facts. A report, originating in London, appeared in the following Canadian press dispatch on March 3:
London, March 3.-Arrangements have been completed for the transportation of 3,000 Sudeten Germans to Canada, it was reported to-night. They will be settled in the Peace River district and in northern Saskatchewan.
The Czech government has agreed to provide the $2,000,000 which the settlers will take to Canada to establish themselves in farming communities. The money came from loans and gifts made by the British and French governments after the Munich settlement.
Canadian railway companies, it is reported, have completed arrangements to take the first group of settlers early in April.
It is understood an agreement has been reached between the Canadian and Czech governments calling for each family to take a minimum of $1,500. The new settlers will be Germans who refused to become citizens of the Reich after the Munich agreement transformed their homes from under the control of Czechoslovakia to that of Germany. They refused to be nazified and voluntarily gave up their homes.
Since the German occupation of the Sudeten areas the men and their women and children have been living under conditions of extreme hardship, with the Czech government providing refugee camps for them.
It is understood a majority of the new settlers are experienced farmers. They will be chosen carefully on behalf of the Canadian government but the total is not expected to exceed 3,000.

maintopic: SUDETEN IMMIGRANTS
subtopic: SETTLEMENT IN CANADA OP FAMILIES FROM CZECHO-SLOVAKIA
speechtext: Was that all a quotation?

maintopic: SUDETEN IMMIGRANTS
subtopic: SETTLEMENT IN CANADA OP FAMILIES FROM CZECHO-SLOVAKIA
speechtext:
Yes, a Canadian press dispatch from London. A Prague dispatch of the fifth instant contained the following:
Prague, March 5.-Eight hundred families of former German socialists and democrats, cut adrift from their homes by Chancellor Hitler's annexation of the Sudetenland, have received permission from Ottawa to establish a village of their own in Canada, it was announced here Saturday.
The Czecho-Slovak and British governments have arranged for approximately 3,000 people to emigrate to the dominion. They will be led by two former members of the Czech Chamber of Deputies, Wenzel Jaksch and Siegfrid Taub.
Reports in London last Friday said the emigrants would be settled in the Peace River district and in northern Saskatchewan. The Prague government has allotted $1,500 to each family. This will come from the $75,000,000 which Britain recently granted Czecho-Slovakia, half as a loan and half as a gift, to aid refugees and assist in reconstruction work. . . ,
Following the partition of Czecho-Slovakia as a result of the Munich settlement, an acute refugee problem arose in Czecho-Slovakia due to the fact that tens of thousands of Czech citizens of German racial origin in the Sudeten area, who had been opposed to the nazi philosophy, fled from their homes in advance of the occupation by German troops. Shortly after this, urgent inquiries were made, from London and Prague, not only of the Canadian but of other governments as well, seeking some relief for these refugees, and Canada was asked if she would take some part in helping to solve the problem. Inquiries were set afoot by our immigration branch to discover the type and background of the refugees, and it was found that they had been engaged mainly in agriculture and small village industries. They were described as a sturdy type, but without capital, since in their flight they had abandoned everything. There were thus two classes-those who might come as agriculturists, a#d those who might come to establish new industries in this country.
When the immigration regulations were amended by order in council in the autumn of 1930, under the previous government, provision was made for the admission of farmers with sufficient means to establish themselves in agriculture in Canada. There has been a movement of such families from year to year, averaging during the past two
169S
Sudeten Immigrants

or three years about five hundred families a year. These have been settled on lands purchased with their own capital, usually farms that had come into the market at a fairly low price. All this settlement has been under the auspices of the colonization branches of our two railways. From reports that the department receives from time to time, it is apparent that the work is being well done. Many of these families have been established successfully with less than SI,500.
Early in December last a delegation from Czecho-Slovakia visited Canada to see if homes could be found for some of these refugees. The delegation consisted of an official of the Czech government and two others representing the German group from the Sudeten area. Their request was fully explored. They were told that, while we could not change the immigration regulations at present in force, no objection would be raised to their inclusion in the movement of agricultural families which has been going on for several years. It was pointed out that they would be required to meet rigid examination overseas as to their physical and mental health and their general fitness for settlement. They were further advised that each family unit-and it was estimated the average family unit was about four-would be required to have on arrival in Canada at least SI,500 of capital.
After this delegation returned to London we were advised that they had succeeded in getting capital whereby these families would be provided with the financial assistance necessary to meet the conditions laid down here, and referred to a moment ago.
Canada has not undertaken any obligation or expenditure in connection with this movement. All the costs of transportation and settlement will come from funds secured from abroad. The actual task of settlement will continue to be undertaken by the colonization branches of the railways. The statement that we have agreed to take 3,000 souls, as the London report suggests, or 800 families, as the Prague report suggests, is pure guess work. We have not agreed to take any specified number. The number to be taken will depend upon the number of those found to be physically and otherwise fit. The examination as to fitness will be hejd overseas, and colonization officials of the railways, together with medical doctors of the department of health, and immigration officials, will cooperate in an effort to see that those who come to Canada will be an asset to this dominion. The examinations will begin shortly. The total number of this group at present in Czecho-Slovakia itself is less than half the number mentioned in press dispatches.

It should be emphasized that such of these families as come to Canada for land settlement will be located under the auspices of the colonization branches of the railways. We have no information at the moment where they will be settled, but we understand that the railways intend putting them into small groups where suitable land is available, in order to make supervision for the first few years less expensive than if they were scattered over wider areas. The report from Prague that these people are coming for village settlement is entirely erroneous.
While the methods being followed for the admission of refugees to Canada may not be satisfactory to all, I believe we are going about the matter in the way best calculated to help some of these unfortunate people, without at the same time disturbing conditions here. Many members of the house know something of the pressure on the department to open the doors wider for the admission of greater numbers than are at present coming in. It is undeniably true that the plight of hundreds of thousands of the refugees in Europe is a desperate one and must appeal to the humanitarian instincts of all. The criticism has been made that, since Canada has vast areas either thinly settled or not settled at all, with a wealth of resources that many other countries envy, we should adopt a more generous attitude in the matter of immigration and give an opportunity to worthy people to make homes for themselves in our fortunate land. We must, however, having regard to existing conditions, recognize that there are limits within which we can assist; within those limits we are trying to deal with these problems with as much consideration as can be given.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, March 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King that the house go into committee on the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the trade agreement entered into at Washington on the 17th day of November, 1938, between Canada and the United States of America, and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned yesterday I was referring to certain industries which had been affected adversely by the Canada-United States trade agreement. In the 1935 agreement only four items of the primary metal group, which would cover such products as bars, rods, plates, sheets, castings and forgings, were affected. In 1937 the imports of those four items amounted to $2,919,000. In the new agreement concessions are made to the United States on some forty items, the imports of which from the United States amounted to $23,000,000 in 1937. The United
1700	COMMONS
Canada-United Stales Trade Agreement
States press release states that the reduction in duty on these items will improve the position of the United States producer in competition with the Canadian manufacturer.
In 1937 Canada imported machinery from the United States to the value of over $50,000,000. These importations did not include items such as aircraft, electrical apparatus, or motor vehicles. Numerous concessions have been made in this field, either the duty being bound or the tariff reduced. In the new agreement certain concessions have been made in the electrical apparatus and machinery group. In 1937 the imports from the United States of these items amounted to nearly $7,000,000. Certain reductions on some of these items were made in the 1935 agreement, and the imports increased from $4,334,000 in 1935 to $7,425,000 in 1937. Total Canadian imports from the United States in 1937 amounted to $491,000,000. The importations of non-agricultural products in that year amounted to $237,000,000. Under the present agreement duty reductions have been made on items which were imported in that year to the extent of $144,000,000. The 1935 rate has been bound on items which were imported in that year to the extent of $45,000,000. The free rate has been bound under the new agreement on items which were imported .to the extent of $48,000,000. These figures do not include imports of, articles the duties on which have been reduced under the most favoured nation clause, and which were imported in 1936 to the value of $74,000,000.
It is quite obvious that the reductions of the tariff and the concessions made in the 1935 agreement resulted in an increase of importations of United States goods into the Canadian market at the expense of the Canadian producers. It is also obvious that the additional concessions and reductions in duty which have been made are going to increase still further United States imports. As the Canadian market is restricted, these importations will be at the expense of the Canadian manufacturer and the Canadian workman.
During the course of the debate on this resolution I believe that the members on this side of the house have been successful in pointing out that the government did not make the proper preparations for the negotiation of such an important treaty, and that the failure to make these preparations seriously handicapped the representatives of the government during the period of negotiation; that the government was woefully ignorant of the economic condition of the industries of this country because it did not consult those industries whose interests have been

affected by the agreement; that the government did not take the same precaution to protect the markets, industries and workmen of Canada as did other countries in the form of quotas and restrictions; that the manufacturing and secondary industries and Canadian workmen have been sacrificed for some temporary and speculative benefit to the cattle and lumbering industries; that the interests of the vegetable and fruit growers have been sacrificed; that this agreement has diverted traffic from Canadian to United States ports; that the government has sacrificed productive revenue in making tariff reductions, which revenue produces purchasing power, and employment, making it necessary to replace this with a non-productive tax which will create unemployment and handicap Canadian industries; that this government has sacrificed part of our British preference in our best markets in wheat, fruits, and lumber; that this agreement will cause grievous harm to our transportation system, railways and steamships, by sending traffic north and south, instead of east and west; that this treaty is not reciprocal, because the United States tariff is much higher on items entering United States markets than the tariff on the same items entering the Canadian market; that this agreement is regarded as a purely economic agreement entered into by the three countries, regardless of the fact that the Canadian government attempts to attach considerable political importance to it in order to hide its faulty workmanship.
In the course of this debate many supporters of the new trade agreement were very much concerned with obtaining the highest possible price for goods produced in their part of the country, and they were equally concerned with paying the lowest possible price for goods purchased in any other part of the country. I do not think this attitude is in the best interests of Canada. According to the Canada Year Book for 1936, there were in Canada 25,491 establishments, employing 582,874 persons, paying out in wages $590,-
326,000,	and producing goods to the net value of $1,302,179,000. About 63 per cent of these workers are dependent on industries that pay about 61 per cent of the total wages and salaries and produce over 51 per cent of the net value of the manufacturing production in Canada. Also dependent on these industries for at least part of their employment are hundreds of engineers, doctors, lawyers, employees of telegraph and telephone companies, railway companies, steamship companies, and those engaged in wholesale or retail distribution.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
Since 1935 this government has been engaged in the policy of reducing tariff protection and granting concessions in such a haphazard manner that the industrialists of this country have not been able to make any plans for the future, and this lack of confidence is reflected in the employment problem. Judging from the fruits of the trade agreements made by this government during the past four years, I think it would be better occupied in devoting more time and energy to developing the internal trade of Canada, equalizing freight rates, and inducing Canadians to buy Canadian coal, Canadian oil, Canadian farm products, and Canadian manufactured products, thus building up a stable market which the government can control, and which will provide greater purchasing power and a higher standard of living, as well as more employment for Canadian workers.
Mr. IV. J. WARD (Dauphin): Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention until a very few days ago to take part in this debate, but believing as I do that this trade treaty is by all odds the most important item to come before parliament this session, if not the most important piece of legislation that has been presented to the Canadian people in this generation, and in view of the attitude of a number of members of the official opposition, including their leader, during the last few weeks, I felt that I owed it to my constituents and to the people of Canada as a whole to express my opinions in respect to this allimportant piece of legislation.
I notice that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) is following well in the footsteps of his predecessor in the number of speeches he is making inside and outside of this house. In his address in Toronto the other day he referred to this government as being a reactionary government. When I think of the opposition to this treaty by the official Conservative party in this house I cannot but feel that they oppose it because the government is too progressive-because we are having too much free trade, they think; because of the government's introduction of penitentiary reform; because of the government's home improvement plan; because of its youth training projects; because of its prairie farm rehabilitation, and because of its various acts with respect to housing and other measures to assist the municipalities. I cannot but think that their opposition was from no other point of view than that the government has been too progressive.
I am going to pay to two or three members of the official opposition the compliment of referring for a few moments to their addresses. I took some notes while the hon. member

for Hamilton East (Mr. Brown) was speaking. One of the things he said was that thousands of men had been thrown out of employment in Hamilton as a result of the 1935 trade treaty-because, in other words, this government had lowered the tariffs on manufactured goods. He went on to say that industries would be put out of business in the city of Hamilton because of the present treaty.
I can only reply that an industry or industries which cannot succeed under the terms of this treaty, substantial though the reductions are that it makes in the duties, is much too expensive a luxury for this country to afford. I say further that an industry that cannot thrive under the duties prevailing in this country at the present time, ranging as they do from 7) to 30 per cent, is certainly too expensive for the country, and their failure must be due to incompetence or to the fact that the industry is not indigenous to the country. I would remind the house that two years ago the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, speaking in this house, stated that there were numerous industries in Canada which should never have been allowed to establish here, that they were not indigenous to the country and had become a very real problem because of the amount of protection they required to enable them to continue to exist.
The hon. member for Hamilton East went on to say that the city of Hamilton paid in wages and salaries $40,000,000 annually. That is a very substantial sum, and we are all proud that the city of Hamilton does provide, through the medium of its industries, that amount of wages and salaries for our Canadian people. But I would remind the hon. member that the little province of Manitoba, which was formerly regarded as the postage stamp province of this dominion, produced from its farms alone from 1926 to 1930 an average yearly production of farm products amounting in value to $622,565,000. After all, therefore, the city of Hamilton, with its $40,000,000 is a very small item in the vast aggregate production of this country.	*
The hon. member also told us that word had come from the west that the west had been sold down the river by this treaty. I would suggest to the hon. member that he remain in his own little back yard because all the information I receive from the west is that they are hoping that nothing will happen to this trade treaty but that it may be given an opportunity to work out fully our economic salvation, and retrieve the lost trade of this country.

The hon. gentleman also spoke of two companies manufacturing washing machines in the city of Hamilton which were put out of business by the 1935 agreement. I can say only this: If there is one item in the domestic trade of Canada where the racket of protection reached a higher degree in the last few years than any other, it was the washing machine manufacturers. I would remind the house that, through the reduction in duties on washing machines which was effected by this government, the price of power machines has been reduced from twenty to forty per cent; and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that throughout the length and breadth of this country the housewives who were previously unable to purchase power machines will thank this government for having reduced the cost of those articles.
I intend to pay the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) the compliment of a reference to his remarks. He also spoke of the industrial workers, and he told the house that forty per cent of Canada's total trade resulted from the Canadian manufacturing interests. He may have made that statement innocently; he may not have known the facts. The facts are that less than twenty-four per cent of the production of this country originates in the secondary industries. I have secured figures as to the number of people engaged in these industries, ranging from the manufacture of needles and pins to the making of locomotives. What do they amount to? From the boy who sweeps the floor to the manager of the factory, they number just 16-1 per cent of all the workers of this country. The total population dependent upon the secondary or manufacturing industries is just 1,771,000. Contrast this with agriculture, in which 3,261,000 are engaged, while in the related natural industries we have actively engaged something over 3,000,000 people. May I refer here to a pamphlet issued by one of the large Canadian grain firms, a concern not interested in the political effects of the tariff policies of any government. The writer points out that there is no hope of restoring the solvency of agriculture in this country until we secure a definite governmental policy in the direction of lower tariffs. I could give a lot more figures, but I do not intend to weary the house, and there are other matters with which I should like to deal. But I should like the hon. members for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) and Waterloo South to realize that only sixteen per cent of the people of Canada are engaged in the secondary industries of this
country, and that only twenty-four per cent of the total wealth production in Canada comes from manufacturing interests.

Well, we measure things by averages in this country. Then I have some further figures that are tremendously interesting. I have taken 147 items purchased by Canadian farmers and compared the cost of these items with the average of farm purchasing power, both based on 1926 as 100. For the period from 1931 to 1935 inclusive the index figure for the items the farmer buys stood at 128, while farm purchasing power was 54, only showing a differential against the farmer during that period of 74. What happened between 1936 and 1938? We find that he paid 130, or 30 above the 1926 level, but that he received 95, or within five of the 1926 level. In other words, based on average values in connection with both production and consumption, the farmers throughout Canada are 35 per cent better off than they were between 1930 and 1935.
Now, I have still another table. I said I would prove that the preference on dominion wheat entering the British market had cost the farmers of Canada many millions of dollars. The wheat policy was just like most of the other terms of the 1932 trade agreement. Let us start with the 1930 grain prices. I have figures before me, again from the bureau of statistics, which show that during 1930 we rode along on a fairly even keel until about September 1, nine days after the Bennett government took office. The trade wrecking crew hadn't got down to work before this date. They did not have their machinery started up. The blasting powder had not been assembled in the depots. They were not quite ready.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
In the 1930 crop year, wheat remained at about the dollar level until about the end of August. And then what happened? In August the price averaged 92 cents. Indeed, the figures I have show that on the day of the election, July 28, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press, the average market price for wheat was 93 cents, for oats 42 cents, for barley 45 cents, for rye 56 cents, and for flax S1.S5. Let us see, however, what the prices were four months later-just four months of the operation of the government that was going to reestablish all things in Canada. In that time wheat had dropped from 93 cents to 67 cents. Oats had dropped from 42 cents to 27 cents; barley, from 45 cents to 31 cents; rye from 56 cents to 33 cents, and flax from $1.85 to $1.22.
In the month of August, 1930, wheat sold at 93 cents, but in September it had dropped to 78 cents. You will recall again, Mr. [M' Ward.]
Speaker, that this was during the time these amateurs were at work. Just one month later, namely in October, it had dropped to 72 cents. In November it was down to 64 cents, and in December, to 55 cents. In other words, wheat had dropped in December to just about half the price it had been in August when the Bennett government took office.
Now we come to the year 1932, when the preference was operating. I would remind hon. members that the treaty became effective on August 22, 1932. At the end of August wheat was selling for 56 cents.
In one month it had dropped to 51 cents; in two months, to 48 cents; in three months, to 46 cents, and one month later to 38 cents. That is what happened under the British preference, and that is why I say that the six per cent preference on Canadian wheat had a disastrous effect upon the wheat growers of western Canada, and instead of bringing them greater returns meant a loss to them of millions of dollars.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be forgiven for not following in my arguments the speech which has just been delivered by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward). I find it difficult to chase phantoms, vapourings and hallucinations. I will give the hon. member one figure, and one only. In December, 1935, the unemployed wage-earners in this country numbered 491,000. In December, 1938, three years after the advent to power of hon. members opposite, the unemployed numbered
472,000,	showing a net reduction of only 19,000 in the number of unemployed wage-earners. In the last three years of the previous administration, namely from December, 1932, to December, 1935, there was a reduction of 221,000 in the number of unemployed, a reduction eleven and a half times as great as hon. members opposite have been able to accomplish. Those, Mr. Speaker, are figures from the bureau of statistics, the source of my hon. friend's figures.
I would remind the hon. gentleman, if I may, that world trade from 1933 to 1935 rose five points of index, whereas world trade from 1935 to 1937 rose twenty points of index. In other words, while world trade was rising only five points of index, unemployment in Canada was reduced by 221,000. and while world trade was rising twenty points of index, unemployment in Canada was reduced by only 19,000. These figures, Mr. Speaker, are also from the bureau of statistics.
I am not so much concerned with such figures as the hon. member has put upon Hansard, or in his use of them as I am con-

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
cerned with this:	Throughout the length and
breadth of Canada there is deepening distress which is, I believe I may say safely to hon. members opposite, a condition which should touch the heart and mind of every hon. member of this house. We should not rise in our places and by the use of "alibis" attempt to dodge that fact. We are faced with that situation. Let us not blink the fact, and let us not make stump speeches which would do credit to "ward" politicians.
I do not purpose at length to prolong the present debate on the resolution before the house. But a sense of responsibility compels me to say a few words at this stage with respect to the ratification of the Canada-United States trade treaty. I have been elected to the house to represent some 70,000 Canadians, the vast majority of whom are dependent upon industry for their livelihood. Accordingly, if a measure is introduced to the house which tends to abridge opportunities for those industrial workers who have sent me to parliament, to say the least I should be derelict in my responsibility if I did not raise my voice in protest on their behalf. Thus I make no apology to the house for speaking in protest against the present trade treaty, at least in so far as it affects the industrial worker. Unemployment, remaining as it has at a staggeringly high figure, and the uncertainty of the future of the young would-be wage-earner, present difficulties which in many cases appear to be insurmountable to the individual. Yet we in this house are being asked to approve a treaty which will deprive many Canadian workmen, now employed, of their jobs.
I shall take as an example one of the industries which are of immediate importance to my constituency. Within a stone's throw of the border of my riding is a leather company which has prospered under reasonable protection and the advantages of the Ottawa agreements of 1932. Until recently some 150 employees have been engaged in this plant in the making of patent leather alone. I am taking this industry only as an illustration. I speak with equal feeling for the security of the jobs of the workmen in any industry, for all the men and women in my riding, yes, in the whole of Canada. I speak for all men and women whose jobs are threatened as a result of the Prime Minister's negotiations at Washington last year.
Hon. members will recall that prior to 1932 an important export from the United States to the United Kingdom was patent leather, in which commodity the United States had nearly 58 per cent of the British market. In 1932 a rate of ten per cent ad valorem was imposed by the United Kingdom against United States patent leather. In 1936 only
11'8 per cent of the British patent leather market was supplied by the United States. The greatest change took place in 1934 when the import duty to the United Kingdom was increased to 15 per cent. Prior to 1932 Canada supplied less than 20 per cent of the patent leather entering the United Kingdom. As a result of the tariff of 1932, and the increase in that tariff in 1934 against the United States, while Canada still had free entry, our share of the British market in this product rose to a total of 76-2 per cent. Under the United States-United Kingdom trade agreement, on August 1, 1939, the duty on patent leather going into the United Kingdom from the United States is to be cut in half, namely tc 7i per cent, which will have the effect ol restoring the market of the United Kingdom to the producers of patent leather in the United States at the expense of the Canadian workman.
I have not taken my opinion alone in this matter. I have discussed it personally with those who, as a result of their identification with this field of industry, are in a position tc know the exact situation and to make an accurate prognosis. Accordingly I state that the jobs of 150 men in the particular firm to which I refer are threatened. On behalf of those who hold those jobs I raise my voice in protest to the Prime Minister of Canada, that in this tripartite treaty our preferred position should be so sacrificed. If I were to take the Prime Minister's advice, which I have no intention of doing, I would go back to my riding and tell these 150 men and women and their families that this agreement was made in the name of patriotism in order tc strengthen the ties between the United Kingdom and the United States, and that they must surrender their jobs and join the ranks of the unemployed in order to bring about a closer union between these two countries That was the advice of the Prime Minister; that is what he told this house. I regret the Prime Minister is not in his seat, but does he honestly feel that such a sacrifice of livelihood is necessary, when these men and women know and when the Prime Minister himself knows that there was not, nor had there been, anything amiss or awry in the relationships between the United Kingdom and the United States?
I wonder if it is patriotic to jeopardize the jobs of Canadian workmen, especially in a time such as this? I wonder if it is patriotic to blink facts? I wonder if it is possible successfully to mix political theories and patriotism? If the relations between the United Kingdom and the United States had been strained, if as a result a treaty had been brought forward to bring together these two
1708	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
nations which had been drifting apart, patriotism and the love of peace might have had to play their part. But I claim it is nothing short of fatuous to state to the people of Canada that men and women should be compelled, because of the action of the right hon. gentleman opposite, to sacrifice their jobs. Certainly his latest trade treaty will make no definite contribution to the friendly relations between the United Kingdom and the United States, about which friendly relations there is definitely not even a shadow of a doubt.
If the Prime Minister of Canada wishes to talk about patriotism, if he wishes to be patriotic; if he in the fullest sense of that noble word wishes to make a contribution to world peace, let him take steps to consolidate and cement even more closely the family of empire and give an indication to the government of the United Kingdom that Canada is still a loyal member of that family. That is the type of patriotism which Canadians from coast to coast will recognize as divorced from party politics.
I shall not take up any more of the time of the house. On behalf of the men and women whose jobs are in jeopardy as a result of this treaty I raise my voice in protest, and in accordance with what I feel to be my responsibility as their representative in this parliament I shall vote against the treaty. In doing so I place my patriotism, my love of empire, my love of peace and my desire to see friendly relations maintained between the United Kingdom and the United States second to those of no man in this chamber, not even excluding the Prime Minister himself.

My sole point is that
his speech is the worst kind of ward politics.
I want to take this first opportunity to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his government upon negotiating the trade treaty that is now before the house. I propose quite frankly to deal with it from the point of view of an industry in which my people are largely and deeply interested. I refer to the fishing industry, and my remarks will deal in toto with the benefits that we expect from this trade treaty.
Perhaps I should preface my remarks with a few figures to indicate the extent of the fishing industry in Canada as a whole. The total value of our fisheries last year was $38,000,000, and we exported approximately $28,000,000 worth, of which $6,000,000 went to the United Kingdom. Some $14,000,000 worth, about fifty per cent of our total exports, went to the United States. Perhaps hon. members will recall the report that Cockfield-Brown and Company made in 1932, in which it was indicated that in Canada the per capita production of fish was 120 pounds, and the per capita domestic consumption only 20'7 pounds. The latter figure has been increased in late years owing to efficient advertising and the progress made in processing and other methods since this government came into power, so that our per capita consumption is to-day approximately 30 pounds. The per capita consumption in Great Britain is 40 pounds; Norway, 70 pounds; Germany, 20 pounds; the West Indies, 33 pounds; Australia, 13 pounds; Ireland, 9 pounds. It will be seen, therefore, that we must export our fishery products in order to live. When it is realized that on the north Atlantic, owing to salinity of water and the conditions as to depth and temperature, we have the largest food fish area in the world, with some 200,000 square miles of fishing grounds adjacent to the maritime provinces, it is easy to see that my fishermen are vitally interested in the export of their products.
We have in the maritime provinces 22,500 fishermen, who produce some 435,000,000 pounds of fish, of a value of $14,500,000 in an average year. Of this $14,500,000 worth, we export in an average year, as recent years go, $7,000,000 worth, or about fifty per cent of our total production to United States. Under present world con-

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
ditions there are only three directions in which our exports can go: the United States, the West Indies and South America, or Europe. Owing to foreign competition, conditions in the West Indies and South America are such that we cannot hope in any large way to enter that market. Disturbed conditions in Europe and increased production by individual countries have shut off that market, so that there is only one direction in which we can hope for increased exports, and that is the United States. There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that so far as the maritime fishermen are concerned, their lifeline is a line of exported fish products to the United States. The importance of marketing our fish in the United States has been recognized by every commission that has investigated fishing conditions in the maritimes-the Duncan commission, the Maclean commission, the Price Spreads commission.
Before going on to the benefits we expect from this trade treaty I should like to make one point clear. Since being a member of this house I have observed a little confusion in the minds of some as to the meaning of the fishing industry. I have heard people say, and representations to this effect have been made to me, that it is simply a matter of going to sea and catching cod or some other kind of fish in the same place and getting the same price all the time. But that is not so.
The fishermen catch different types of fish; they fish in different areas; they market their catch differently and get different prices. In considering a trade treaty such as this, therefore, it is well to look at it from the point of view of this group of industries rather than to concentrate on one particular detail and judge the treaty from that basis alone.
In order to see at a glance the concessions which this treaty makes on fish and fish products of the Atlantic coast, I have prepared a schedule indicating the 1930 tariff, the new treaty rate, with proportional reduction, as well as the quantity and value of our fish shipped to the United States in 1937, and the duty paid, according to the United States figures. The schedule is not a long one, and rather than take the time to read it I would ask your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, to place it on Hansard.

It will be seen from this schedule that the reductions have been from twenty-five to fifty per cent on practically every dutiable fish of any importance. It is important in that regard to remember that we can obtain as a maximum only a fifty per cent reduction, because the President of the United States in negotiating a trade treaty cannot go beyond a fifty per cent reduction from the existing tariff; that is the 1930 tariff. Having in mind the opposition that existed for some time in the United States to any reduction whatever on fishery items, a study of the reductions made by this treaty shows that our negotiators must have had a touch of genius to obtain the concessions they did. I well remember that back in 1933 a group of United States sea captains went aboard the Thibault, as a fishing delegation, directly to Washington to protest against any reduction in the duty on fishery items. I remember how they were met, and we in the maritimes are particularly sensitive to these things. One of the commissioners made this statement, and I have never forgotten it since the day I read it, because, as I saw it at least, it meant prosperity or depression to our Canadian fishermen. This was the statement Commissioner Page made to the delegates and to Captain Morrissey, as a result of their conference: "Our sympathies are absolutely with you. If there is anything we can do, you can count upon us". But that was a death blow to the Canadian fishermen at that time so far as obtaining concessions was concerned. Following the opposition in that country there was never a reduction of major importance up to the present time. An efficient campaign was organized by the national fisheries association, and notwithstanding all the obstacles, we obtained the concessions which appear in the schedules that have already been referred to.
The people of the maritimes understood the difficulties and fully appreciated the situation. They are thankful for the efforts which have been made and the results which have been obtained. The 1930 tariff can be said to have meant generally the protection of United States fishermen on certain species of fish during periods of abundant domestic 
production, permitting the marketing of Canadian products during periods only of scarcity in the United States. The reductions in the tariff as we have them to-day will, I believe, have these three effects. First, we are going to see an increased export to the United States during periods of scarcity. Second, we are going to see increased exports during periods of United States production. Third, we are going to have the benefits of reductions on the same volume of business that we had before the treaty. I do not believe for a moment that we are going to glut the United States market. Our equipment and our production are not such as would enable that to be done under ordinary circumstances. Supply and demand in the United States will, I believe, control the United States production, and we shall fit into that general picture.
It is difficult, of course, to foretell in dollars and cents how far exports to the United States will increase. While tariff reductions are the most important element, another factor is the capacity of our fish dealers and merchants and fishermen to take advantage of the reduction; also, conditions in the United States will have a great deal to do in determining the extent of our increased business. There are bound to 'be increases' under these items, and those increases will benefit the individual fishermen, of the kind of whom I have a large number in my constituency, and whom I keep in mind at all times. Up to the present these men have been operating under great difficulties. I hope and believe that these concessions will relieve them of those difficulties and enable them to carry on with a greater profit.
In considering the effects of this treaty it is important to know something of the history of past changes in tariffs with the United States. I intend hurriedly to go over them.
The first major change between Canada and the United States was under the treaty which lasted from 1S54 to 1866. We had free entry of fish into the United States, and our exports to that country doubled during that time.
The next phase was under the treaty of Washington. Again we had free entry of fish. In 1872 the value of our exports of fish to the United States was $1,336,000; when the treaty expired in 1885, it was $2,579,000. As a result of the termination of that treaty, and because of lack of the market which had been provided under the previous treaty, in the province of Nova Scotia alone 2,400 men dropped out of the fishing industry.
The next major change was in 1898, when, after the Spanish-Ameriean war, Puerto Rico went to the United States and tariffs were
raised. As a result of the restriction of markets our fishing industry lost 1,064 men in Nova Scotia alone.	.
The next major change in tariffs was in 1914, when free entry of fish into the United States was provided for under the Underwood tariff. In the previous year our exports of fish to the United States amounted to $6,914,000; by 1919 they had increased to $18,560,000.	,
As a result of the Fordney-McCumber tariff of 1921 business again dropped. Our sales of fish decreased from $18,560,000 in 1920 to $16,750,000 in 1929, and 2,700 Nova Scotians had to leave the industry.
As a consequence of the prohibitive 1930 tariff there was again a fall in our exports to the United States, from $16,750,000 in 1929 to $11,430,000 in 1931. Because of these two tariffs, the Fordney-McCumber and Hawley-Smoot tariffs, in the port of Yarmouth alone a fleet of more than twenty vessels was wiped out. It was impossible for our fishermen successfully to prosecute the industry under those conditions. Generally speaking, over this period of years the up or down movement of the United States tariff has meant the decrease or increase of our exports to that
country.	. .
So far as I can see, in the mantimes this treaty has been well received, not only by Liberals but by every sincere and well meaning Conservative, by all the better thinking people, by those who have at heart the real interests of the fishing industry. Criticism comes only from three selfish groups-I think that is a fair way to describe them. They are types which can be put into one or other of these pigeonholes. The first type of individual is he who is dealing in only one kind of fish. At the outset I referred to this element in the industry. What he wants is something like Santa Claus something which would enable him to go into every market in the world free of duty and sell fish without competition from other countries. All you will hear from that sort of person is criticism of just one detail, and from a selfish standpoint.
The second kind of critics is composed of a very few fish merchants who are anxious to get cheap fish from the fishermen. There are really very few of these among the merchants carrying on a sort of whispering campaign against this treaty. They are against the treaty because they want to continue to buy cheap fish; they are afraid that, with this added market, the fisherman will command a better price and will make them pay more for his fish.
The third sort of person from whom you hear criticism is the one who, because of political malice, has lost all sense of sincerity.

of the opportunities they had in negotiations in that period, we would have had free fish fifteen years ago. The United States, under the Underwood tariff, had given us free fish. They made representations asking our government to allow United States vessels to enter our ports. The Canadian government of that day, I submit quite negligently, lost this opportunity of concluding a treaty with the United States that would have given us free entry for our fish for fifteen years and another two years thereafter if notice of termination had been given. I should like to refer to the report of the conference between Canada and the United States, dated September 6, 1918, and dealing with fishery items. After referring to a number of matters this unanimous report was made:
In the light of these facts your commissioners feel constrained to recommend that the Canadian duty on fresh and frozen fish not including shell fish be removed and with a view to assuring stability in the industry that the two countries enter into an agreement by which such fish will be admitted customs duty free from either country into the other, and that such arrangement remain in force for fifteen years, and thereafter until two years after the date when either party thereto shall give notice to the other of its wish to terminate the same.
I have gone into this matter very carefully, and I think if the government of that day had felt towards the fishermen as the present government feels, we would have had a fifteen-year treaty between the two countries providing for the free entry of fish, and the wishes of my hon. friend, who said that fifteen years ago tariff reductions would have been good, would have been fulfilled. When I think of the pressure that was exerted by the present government on behalf of the fishermen in the negotiation of this treaty, and compare it with the lack of interest and understanding shown by the government of 1916-20, I can see what is going to happen to this treaty when the testing time comes. The fishermen of the maritime provinces will see prominently displayed on the banner of hon. gentlemen opposite the slogan "No truck or trade with the Yankees." They realize that the Conservative party is not in favour of the reductions in tariff that have been made.
I disagree with my hon. friend when he says, as his last point, that no benefits will be derived by the individual fishermen. I think we are going to have an increase in production and also, we believe, increased revenues, so that in my opinion the fishermen will benefit from this treaty in very large measure. As an illustration I mentioned that our exports to the United States amounted to
$7,000,000, half of which is dutiable and the other half free. If under this treaty we can increase the $3,500,000 that is dutiable to thrice that amount or more, it will mean that the value of our production will be increased from $14,500,000 to $20,500,000, which in turn will mean one-third more revenue to the industry as a whole. When it is remembered that this will entail practically no increase in capital cost to the fishermen, it will be seen that this will be of great benefit to them.
For a number of years past I have realized the seriousness of the situation in which our fishermen found themselves. In 1937 I stated that unless something was done we would have on the shores of the maritime provinces deserted villages with gaping cellars as monuments of bygone days. I still think that was true. I have followed the gradual trend of the satisfied and self-contained community of former days to the village or district inhabited by poor, discouraged and rather hopeless individuals who had lost every sense of security and all hope for the future. In some instances there has been an improvement since the dark days of 1933. Mr. Speaker, when this treaty was announced some months ago I gave expression to the view that any measure that would improve economic conditions as between Canada and the United States, or that would assist in improving the relationship existing between the United States and Great Britain, would be a worth-while effort and a good move. But I qualified that by saying that it would all depend on the terms of the treaty and the basis upon which it was negotiated and consummated. It is my intention this afternoon to approach this question, I hope without too much prejudice but with a view to analysing within the brief time at my disposal the background not only of the treaty but also of the relationship existing between Canada and the United States. By "background" of course I mean economically.
1714	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
Fortunately the national and social background is all that one could desire, and of it we are all exceedingly proud. It is the economic background with which I desire to deal, having regard to the possible effect of this treaty upon Canada's trade policy as a whole.
Reference has been made, particularly by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as well as by many other hon. members, to what has been termed the prevalence of economic nationalism in the world to-dajr, and that has been deplored. I am not going to enter upon any very extensive discussion as to whether that is good or bad, but it has been introduced and referred to repeatedly during the debate on this treaty. Furthermore, and this is why I mentioned the first point, it also has been stated that the agreements entered into at the economic conference of 1932 contributed to or aggravated the trend to economic nationalism.
With that contention I take distinct issue, and I propose to deal with it somewhat briefly. Before doing so, however, it seems to me there is a contradiction in the attitude of many hon. members who have spoken in [DOT] support of the treaty. On the one hand it is argued that Canada was justified in giving concessions-and the word "sacrifices" has been used-because that contributed to the improved relationship between the United States and the United Kingdom. That is one presentation. On the other hand it is argued that Canada is realizing very marked benefits from this treaty. It must be obvious, Mr. Speaker, that you cannot take both positions. On the one hand if we are going to claim that we have been broad-minded and generous and have made sacrifices in the interests of this international amity about which we hear so much, certainly on the other hand we cannot claim that we have obtained some rich benefits out of the thing for which we sacrificed ourselves. So obviously there is considerable inconsistency in the attitude of those who support the treaty.
Now let me deal briefly with this argument that the imperial economic agreements of 1932 contributed to the extension of economic nationalism. I do not think Canada or Great Britain can be blamed in any sense whatever for economic nationalism. For no country did more, or attempted to do more to promote international amity and goodwill in the world during the last fifteen or twenty years, since the war, than did Great Britain. And certainly Canada has not done anything towards the promotion of economic nationalism in the world. Let it be remembered 
that Great Britain risked everything. She risked her national existence in the interests of peace and disarmament. Year after year, and year after year, the British parliament went on participating in disarmament agreements, scrapping warships and other warlike material to the value of hundreds of millions of pounds, in the hope that the rest of the world would join in on a general policy of disarmament. And, sir, to say that Great Britain and Canada and the other dominions of the empire which joined in the Ottawa conference are responsible in any way or in any degree for economic nationalism, is a blight upon the honour, the goodwill and the good faith of Great Britain and the dominions of the British empire.
What are the facts? The facts are that following the great war-and I want to emphasize this-all down through those years, around 1923 and 1924, country after country introduced entirely new methods of international trade, forced upon them by internal conditions. Remember: I am not criticizing those countries for what they did. They did it in self defence, and out of a sense of self preservation. Those European countries- Italy, France, Germany, Austria, Poland, Roumania, Bulgaria, Greece, and other countries particularly of Europe, as well as elsewhere-learned during the war very feevere lessons as to being unprepared economically to face conditions which in fact did arise out of the last war and might arise out of a second war.
And so country after country, based upon fear and experience, introduced new methods to cope with their internal difficulties. For instance, the record was placed upon Hansard by me several years ago with respect to Italy. Italy, one of our prominent customers, in 1923 put inhibitions and quotas upon a whole list of articles, and thereby seriously affected our trade with that country-a trade which used to be extensive. That trade has now fallen down to small figures. The decrease began in 1923; it was not after the intra-imperial agreements, at all.
We know what Russia has done; we know what Germany did. Germany, of course, was forced to it not only by economic conditions of the country but also by international exchange. The same is true of other countries; there has been difficulty in connection with getting external exchange to meet their obligations abroad. These are the factors which have forced such countries as Italy, Germany, Russia, the Netherlands and other central European countries to which I have referred to adopt extreme measures in dealing with their foreign trade policy. And it

Canada-United States
Trade Agreement
was the introduction of these quotas, internal taxes, prohibitions, and various strange devices, plus the necessity for exchange or,
I should say, the collapse of international exchange-it was all that, based upon stark fear, that was the cause of the dislocation of external trade. And it was not, I would ask the house to remember, until more than ten years after the war that the Ottawa agreements were made. Therefore to say that those agreements made at Ottawa had anything to do with the promotion of world nationalism is a statement, I believe, without foundation.
It has been asked, and particularly by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McKenzie)-to use his words-"What is the use of debating this treaty?" "Why should we waste the time of the house debating the treaty? It is in force, and you can do nothing about it.'5 That is perfectly true; the treaty is in force, and nothing we can do will change it; I am satisfied of that. But, to say that that is a reason why we should be silent and not discuss this all important matter is of course ridiculous. It would be a negation of parliamentary duties and responsibilities.
I make no apologies for discussing the treaty. I believe it ought to be discussed as dispassionately and as intelligently as we can. We ought to consider the various parts of it, and we ought to discuss the major policy involved.
I want to say that in my opinion the treaty is going to have very definite and serious effects upon our external trade policy generally. Time alone will tell whether by and large, on balance, it will be beneficial or adverse. But there is no question that hon. members on either side of the house have a perfect right to express their views in the matter. That it will affect our trade with the British empire and with thirty-eight other countries, very definitely and very directly, cannot be questioned. I say that because the treaty deals with the most favoured nation proposal, or policy, which affects the trade of thirty-eight different countries to which I shall refer in a minute.
I propose to discuss the treaty from two main aspects, first as to its effect from the most favoured nation clause, and also from the financial standpoint. Perhaps before saying anything more with respect to most favoured nation treatment I might read the definition given by authorities in the customs branch. The definition of "most favoured nations" as it appears in the schedule to the customs tariff is as follows:

shall not be subjected to higher duties or charges than those paid on like articles the produce or manufacture of any foreign countries.
That' is a clear, succinct definition of what we mean when we refer to most favoured nation treatment. What I am asking myself is this-and I know it is a very serious question: Did the government take care to understand and apprise themselves of the full effect of the reductions upon their trade with these other, countries? It may be argued that at the present time our foreign trade is favourable to Canada. That is true. And it may therefore be argued that if we do extend the same advantages to these countries no one could complain. But there is this feature to consider: In a world which is trading to-day under bilateral agreements, in a world where nearly every country with which we deal uses quotas, inhibitions

Trade Agreement
and prohibitions of one kind or another, for Canada to, shall I say, disarm itself entirely by voluntarily giving those countries access to this territory on the full list included in this and other treaties, without receiving back from those countries one single concession-I say for us to put ourselves in that position is in my opinion a decided and definite weakness.
Let me repeat. Other countries are basing their external trade largely upon bilateral agreements, that is, agreements by which one country gives a concession for a like concession on the part of the other. We, on the other hand, have made this treaty with the United States, and every last benefit in it will be given to these other thirty-eight countries, with not a single concession being granted to us in return. Not only that, but we have no concession to offer to them. If to-morrow we try to make a trade treaty with Italy, Germany or any one of the countries the names of which I have read, and ask for some concession, that country will reply, "What have you to offer?" They will tell us that they already have the full advantage of our intermediate tariff, that they already have the full advantage of all we have given the United States, France and all these other countries. I submit that we have tied our hands so that we can have no expectation of working out bilateral agreements.
Some years ago when I was still Minister of Trade and Commerce I had in mind the abandonment of the most favoured nation policy in connection with Canadian trade. Our trade is largely with the British empire and the United States, the balance being comparatively small although not unimportant.

For us to give away all our trading advantages, to release the others fiom the necessity of making concessions to us, seems to me to be an exceedingly questionable policy. I have in my hand a publication issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce and dated 1938, and I ask hon. members to listen to some excerpts which I shall read. They have heard me read the list of countries which have the most favoured nation advantage. This is what this publication has to say regarding most favoured nation agreements :
Ihe benefit to Canadian exports of mostfavoured-nation treatment in any country depends on the customs and treaty system of the particular importing country concerned.
This is the present government speaking through its own publication. Of the countries I have mentioned, eleven have a single 
tariff which is open to all countries. In other words, we get no advantage over any other country. With minor exceptions, Argentina applies her tariff equally to imports from all countries. Belgium has a minimum tariff which in practice is applied equally to imports from all countries. The customs duties of Bolivia are applied equally to imports from all countries. Denmark has a single tariff schedule, and the general tariff of Italy is applicable to imports from all countries. The Netherlands has a single tariff schedule without tariff preference to any country. Norway has a single tariff schedule, and the duties of Panama apply equally to imports from all countries. Sweden has commercial treaties with various countries and has granted conventional rates of duties which, however, have been incorporated into her ordinary tariff and made applicable to all countries. Switzerland operates under a single column tariff which applies to all countries, and no preferences exist under the tariff of Venezuela. This policy by these countries of attempting to give parity to all countries makes the binding of the most favoured nation clause meaningless. My submission is that we could well afford to consider again the advisability of casting aside the most favoured nation policy as far as Canada is concerned.
I dislike quoting, but for the purpose of the record I think I should read what the United States press release had to say as to the effects of the most favoured nation feature of this treaty upon the trade of Canada. I quote:
The actual effect, therefore, was an enduring reduction in rates on a large volume of trade.
Ihe concession by Canada of most-favourednation treatment meant much more than the mere removal of the differentials which iormerly existed against American goods as compared with the goods of most other non-*riA!sh.countries. A much greater gain lay m the fact that the lower rates resulting from that provision improved the position of American producers in competition with Canadian producers of the same commodities.
That is the point in this treaty that appeals to the United States government. Then they go on to say:
There are still hundreds of items in the Canadian tariff with respect to which the United States benefits directly by the mostfavoured-nation provision-items on which the rates now being paid are lower than before 1936 solely by virtue of this provision. The imports of this group from the United States in 1937 amounted to $79,000,000.
They refer there to the hundreds of items which are in addition to those specified in the schedule to the treaty. In other words, over and above all the schedules, the United States has, by virtue of the inclusion of the most

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
favoured nation clause in this treaty, an advantage in trade which in 1937 amounted to $79,000,000.
I should like to refer briefly to the question of dumping, because the dumping provision has a part in this whole set-up. We have in our tariff law a section which was placed there by a distinguished minister of the Laurier government, the late Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, who is recognized as having been one of the outstanding finance ministers of Canada. He was a man whom I knew well and respected most highly. He introduced into the Canadian tariff a policy which I am sorry to say is scoffed at to-day by the Liberal party. It is not applied energetically by the government, and yet it is one of the soundest provisions in the tariff structure of this country. I refer to section 6 of the customs tariff, known as the dumping clause. What is the history of the dumping clause? I would invite the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) and others who talk so, shall I say recklessly, about the desire of certain industries to have protection, to study the history of this clause and the doctrine which lies behind it. If they did that, I think we would hear much less railing against importers and the policy of protection in Canada. At the risk of being tedious I am going to read this section into the record.
I remind the house that I conceive it to be one of the soundest pieces of doctrine ever introduced into the customs laws of this country. Section 6 reads:
In the case of articles exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value of the same article [DOT] when sold for home consumption in the usual and ordinary course in the country whence exported to Canada at the time of its exportation to Canada, or is less than the fair market value or value for duty thereof as determined under the provisions of section thirty-six of the Customs Act-
That latter part is later than Mr. Fielding's time.
-or is less than the value for duty thereof as determined bv the minister ... or is less than the fair market value thereof as fixed under the provisions of section forty-three of the Customs Act, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such article, on its importation into Canada, a special or dumping duty, equal to the difference between the said selling price of the article for export and the said fair market value thereof or value for duty thereof.
Now there are goods being imported from the United States at the present time-and from other countries as well, I think, but I have reference particularly to the United States-which are being sold in Canada for
less than the fair market value in the United States; and they are entering this country in large quantities. It is a question of administration; it is not a question of Tory protection or any other form of Tory doctrine. These goods are coming in, as they have been for over thirty years, contrary to the laws of Canada, and contrary to the doctrine introduced into the laws of this country by a Liberal finance minister whose authority no Liberal member of this house would question. Yet these goods continue to come in here in definance of the law as it stands, and to the injury of Canadian production.
For example, there is a certain machine in common household use. I am not going to mention it because I do not wish to give particular instances here, for this is not the place. But a certain manufacturer in the United States makes a small number of cheap machines, less than ten per cent of his output, which are advertised for sale at about half the regular price of his general production. They get the advantage of low-price advertising. The aim is to attract interest in his product, and this firm will discharge a salesman if he sells one of these machines, or more than one, in a district in the United States. The salesmen must sell only the higher priced machine there. They can quote on the other, but all sorts of difficulties are put in the way of delivery, and they do not sell the cheap machine in the United States. They are, however, shipped into Canada and sold here in competition with our own products at a loss to the manufacturer in the United States, although they are listed there in an attempt to comply with this law. In my opinion, that i3 the sort of thing we are going to suffer from when this treaty comes into force because it covers a great many articles of that kind. I have merely cited one case as an illustration.
I should like now to refer briefly to the point I made a moment ago as to the difficulties of doing external trade in these days. I have before me an article written by the Hon. Rupert E. Beckett, and published in the Monetary Times of March 4 last, and I quote it because it is an excellent illustration of the difficulties to which I have referred and which, I warn the house and I warn the government, will, if we are not very careful, arise from this treaty because of its most favoured nation feature:
In many other countries where British interests were well established, particularly in southeastern Europe and South America, they have been seriously jeopardized by the intrusion of political considerations and influences into the economic sphere. Fair competition British

traders can meet, but to-day the destination of business is frequently decided not by competitive efficiency but by political manoeuvres and considerations of national expediency.

A new, and more subtle, form of trading has come into vogue, in which one country undertakes to absorb another's output of a particular crop or material. A primary producing country naturally finds the prospect of securing an assured market for its products an alluring one, but in practice the interchange has proved to have considerable drawbacks. The dominant partner in the agreement, whilst itself receiving much-needed raw materials, has been able to dump inferior or unwanted goods on the other.
I quote that merely for the purpose of emphasizing the dangers of the most favoured nation feature of this agreement.

In regard to these matters I had some serious and definite views which I was prepared to offer, not in any captious or partisan manner, but simply because I am absolutely convinced that this country must face these issues. Moreover, in 1925 I pointed out to the house that if we pursued the policy we were then pursuing, and are still pursuing, in connection with our trade with the United States, sooner or later we would reach a point where we would be economically shackled and bound to that country-and we have pretty nearly reached that stage.
When this treaty was being negotiated we should have taken up with the government of the United States the whole question of our economic relationship. We should have pointed out to them that we owed the United States, as I can show, in the neighbourhood of four and a half billion dollars, on which interest has to be paid. There are heavy capital investments in Canada which must be returned

I want to call attention to a few figures. In the years from 1926 to 1938 we imported from the United States $6,516,000,000 worth of goods. In the same period we exported to them $4,285,000,000 worth of goods. In other words, there was an adverse balance of trade of some two billions of dollars in those thirteen years. Not only is that the case, but I want to impress on the house this fact, that while we can go on frittering away our patrimony for a long time yet because undoubtedly we have vast resources in this country, sooner or later we shall have to face this situation. I repeat, that in those thirteen years we have had an adverse balance of trade with the United States of $2,200,000,000, in addition to which we have to pay over $200,000,000 a year in interest. We cannot escape that fact.
This situation ought to be reviewed. I do not think it is saying anything unkind of the United States to say this, that they must realize that we are one of their heavy debtors and that we are among the best customers they have. It is not my intention to analyse in detail the trade agreement which is at present the subject of discussion before this house. Last year I was unfortunately absent from the house when the budget was presented and debated. I was, however, able to express privately my views to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and other members of the government and, frankly, the budget of last year was disappointing to me. I believe also it was disappointing to the government itself. The government had hoped before parliament prorogued last year to be in a position to present the trade agreement, but owing to prolonged negotiations, over much of which there was no control in Canada, the date when the trade agreement was finally consummated was subsequent to prorogation. Because I was disappointed, and perhaps even somewhat critical with respect to the budget, I feel it all the more incumbent upon me now to express my views in connection with this trade agreement. I realized last year, and so stated, that it might be unwise, indeed probably would be unwise, to make some slight alterations in the tariff while at that time negotiations were under way regarding this trade agreement.
I am in complete accord with bilateral trade agreements, but as a Liberal I cannot accept the view that it is only in that way that tariff changes should be effected. If at any time it is in the interests of this country to reduce the tariff on any article entering Canada, that tariff should be reduced, whether or not there is any so-called concession given by another country. Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) referred to unilateral changes in the tariff, and considered them unwise, at least at that time. While I am in perfect sympathy with bilateral agreements, I must insist that at all times when downward revisions of the tariff can be made in the interests of this country, they should be made, irrespective of any concessions received from any other country.
As a member of the Liberal party I am indeed proud of the achievement of our government in concluding what is perhaps the most extensive and favourable trade agreement which has been made by Canada during this century, indeed perhaps since confederation. I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister upon his able presentation to

this house in connection with this trade agreement. I have also listened to or read other excellent contributions to the debate, but I should like to make special mention of the address delivered by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley). He made a clear, concise and convincing review of the benefits which will accrue to Canada under this agreement.
This debate reveals clearly the different points of view between the parties represented in this house. Members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, both in the house and outside it, have from time to time been proclaiming that there is really no difference between the policy of the Liberal party and the policy of the Conservative party, that they are really so much alike that they might be regarded as having a distinction without any difference. No doubt those hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party were making those speeches for political effect. They tried to make the people of the country believe that, after all is said and done, these two great old parties have drifted together so closely that they are now really as one, and that now the party really opposing them is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party.
Well, let us look at the situation as we have it before us in the house at the present time. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) and his party not only have been extremely critical of the agreement as a whole, but have picked out individual items here and there stating that they would adversely affect their part of the country, and inferentially endeavouring to lead the house and the country to conclude that the trade agreement as a whole is not in the interests of this country.
What is the history of the parties with respect to trade agreements? The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) went back nearly half a century in an endeavour to show that certain persons in the United States held views which, in his judgment, were inimical to that republic having closer trade relationships with Canada. He also quoted certain unfortunate remarks of United States statesmen in connection with the reciprocal trade agreement arranged by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding.
