The Tories have always had a great faculty of waving the flag to prevent Liberal governments from taking away some of the special privileges from the few in an endeavour to deal in a fair and just way with the masses of the people and with the consumers of Canada.
Let us look at the negotiations which took place between Canada and the United States in connection with consummating a trade agreement when the Conservative party was in power under the leadership of the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett. How far did they progress? Just to the point where it would be advantageous for political purposes. The public did not have, could not have, any knowledge, of what the proposed agreement was; it could be used in various parts of the country for political effect, and Conservative speakers would draw on their imagination as to the content of the agreement, according to the feeling of the people in the locality where such speeches were made.
But what is the important point? The agreement was not consummated by the Conservative party. Within a very few weeks after the Liberal party came into power in 1935, a reciprocal trade agreement was consummated. During the discussion of that trade agreement in this house it became abundantly clear that the Conservative party was not at any time really in favour of a trade agreement, and that was why it had not been signed the previous year.
What is the attitude to-day of the leader of the opposition? Is he for this trade agreement? Not only he, but every hon. member of this house, will be called upon to say whether he is for or against this trade agreement, and I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that at the conclusion of this debate, when the vote is taken, the people of this country will know in more certain fashion than ever before just where the parties of this country really stand on fiscal policy. Members of the Tory party have been saying in the house, and
particularly outside the house in different sections of the country where they believe it would be more beneficial to them, that they were in favour of trade agreements, that they were in favour of wider trading with other countries. If that be true, they will have an opportunity in this house within the next day or two, perhaps within the next few hours, to demonstrate to the Canadian people that they really believe in a greater opportunity for the interchange of goods with other countries. The leader of the opposition said as to this agreement, that only time could tell whether it is good or whether it is not. I ask him, and I ask every member of his party, this question: Are they prepared to give this trade agreement such an opportunity, so that time will tell? If they vote against this agreement, and if by any chance their vote should prevent it from becoming law, my question is, how will time tell? If they succeed in voting down this resolution-

speechtext:
I have looked over this trade agreement and I find there benefits for farmers, benefits for lumber men, benefits for fishermen, benefits for various classes, but I find further that there are benefits for every Canadian consumer, which means benefits for every man, woman and child in this country. The Liberal party promised the people of Canada that tariffs would be reduced to the level of the Dunning budget. I am happy to say that a close study of this agreement reveals that on practically everything the duty has been reduced to the level of the Dunning budget of 1930, and, in many instances, has gone much beyond that point.
Take, for example, farm machinery. Under the Dunning budget there were certain items at six per cent, others at 7\ per cent, and still others at ten per cent. Under this agreement the tariff on all farm machinery has been reduced to 71 per cent. There have been
1722	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
some who have already said, " Yes, duties have been reduced, but when they were reduced the prices of farm machinery were not reduced, they were increased." I regret to say that prices were somewhat higher. Recently these prices have been reduced to a certain extent. After the extensive investigation which a committee of this house made with respect to the farm implement industry of Canada, and the corresponding investigation made by a similar committee of the congress of the United States, it was clearly disclosed that no manufacturer of farm implements prepared his price list until the largest manufacturing company in both countries had brought down its price lists. In Canada there is every appearance that there is, if not a definite combination in restraint of trade, at least a complete understanding that prices shall not be reduced below an agreed level.
I should like to say now to the government and to this house that this is a matter which in the immediate future should receive the most careful scrutiny, and if the evidence warrants it, prosecution should be undertaken against any firms who in an unlawful combination act together to maintain unwarranted prices for farm machinery, or for any other goods.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing the attitude of the various parties towards the trade agreement. I sometimes listen with interest to the speeches of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Sometimes he makes a good speech; sometimes he talks like a Liberal, and I ask myself why he is sitting in that corner. As 1 have said already, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation speakers refer to the two old parties as being alike, that they are on the same road, which I might call the road of trade. It is important that we examine carefully whether or not this is true. It may be that these parties are on the same road, but let us look more closely. A couple of years ago, with my wife, I took an extended automobile trip through the United States. We travelled over wonderful roads, extremely well marked. If you followed the road bearing your particular number you might arrive at your destination, but there was one thing which that number did not give, and that was the direction. If you neglected that and

went the wrong way you would end up at a point opposite to that of choice. The Liberals and Conservatives may be on the same road, but they are going in opposite directions. That is the difference which the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation speakers do not point out. The direction the Conservative party has always followed leads to the building up of impediments to international trade, to the blocking of international trade, while the Liberals have always gone in the opposite direction, that of the lowering or the removal of impediments to international trade.
Where do the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members stand? Do they favour the Tory or the Liberal direction? My only objection, if I have one, to the course pursued by the Liberal party concerns neither the road nor the direction, but rather the speed with which they travel. I should like to get into high gear and go faster. It may be that no party is willing to travel at the rate at which I am prepared to go. If my Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends were really anxious to see the Liberals go a bit faster, would it not be better for them to join the Liberal party and assist those of us who are trying to get as far as possible in the right direction with the least delay? The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members come from western Canada, and all they have succeeded in doing is dividing western influence and delaying progress. Heaven forbid that I should raise an east-west issue. I do not believe in that. I believe in a united Canada. At the same time there is such a thing as a balanced policy, the best policy having regard to Canada as a whole, and western opinion should not be divided in its influence. In my judgment this division of opinion has been a great detriment to western Canada. In a democracy such as ours I do not believe it is in the public interest that there should be more than two parties in this country, and the public is beginning to share that view if one is to judge from the small number of Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members returned at the last election.
I am happy to support this extensive trade agreement. It is not only on the right road, facing the right direction; it has gone a long distance in that direction, and I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his government upon the success of their efforts. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says he will support this agreement, and other Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members have said the same thing. I ask this question: What part did they have in urging fonvard and assisting with the agreement? They have done nothing; in fact,

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
both within and without this house Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members have rather belittled the idea that there was much advantage in extending international trade. They have advanced the notion that the thing to do is to socialize the whole state. Why will my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar support this agreement? He does not dare oppose it, or whatever chance he may have of reelection to this house would be entirely removed; h'e would not have the ghost of a chance for reelection. He did nothing to assist in bringing about this agreement, yet I suppose he will go back to his constituency and tell how he helped his people.
I should now like to say just a word to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). Where does he stand on this question? I put that squarely to him, although I see he is not in his seat. Do the people of the constituency of Qu'Appelle believe in a better opportunity to exchange the goods which they do not require for the goods of other countries? I venture the opinion that there is not one person in his constituency who does not approve this agreement taken as a whole. The people of Qu'Appelle, together with the people of this whole country, will watch this vote more keenly than they have watched any other vote ever taken in this house. Now that we have a chance to advance the interests of our country-for this agreement is in the interests of the whole of Canada-let us do our duty as citizens and not think in terms of party. I say this to my Tory friends, who deep down in their hearts know that this agreement is in Canada's interests. It is also true that it is in the interests of the other party to the agreement', the United States; and any agreement, if it is to be counted good, must be mutually beneficial.
I commend the government also for the part they played in assisting in the negotiations between the United States and the United Kingdom. I desire to emphasize especially that part of the Prime Minister's address in this house in which he made it clear that Canada was willing to negotiate agreements not only with the United States and members of the British commonwealth but with all countries willing to trade with us on a fair and equitable basis. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) rather poked fun at the reference by the Prime Minister to the effect of such agreements on the peace of the world, and amused himself by referring to the peaceful boundary line between us and our great and friendly neighbour. He knew the Prime Minister was not thinking about any disturbance between these two countries but was referring to Great Britain, the United States and Canada pointing the way to international goodwill by means of greater international trade, and holding this out as a beacon light for the whole world to follow. If the example of these nations who have concluded these agreements were followed by the whole world, it would lead to international goodwill, to the cessation of the suicidal race to rearm, and to the removal of the causes which lead to war. It was this wider sphere to which the Prime Minister referred. It is interesting to note British public opinion in connection with the trade agreement. I quote from the London Spectator of November 25, 1938:
In the simple but significant ceremony that attended the signature of the Anglo-American trade treaty at Washington last week the just comment was supplied, very fitly, by the Prime Minister of Canada, Mr. Mackenzie King, when he said that "it must be increasingly apparent that the stability of the civilization which we cherish depends more than ever on the friendly association of the English-speaking nations of the old world and the new.
That assertion deserves study in some detail, for it states an important truth with singular accuracy. The English-speaking nations . . . are to-day in a special sense the trustees of the only kind of civilization their own citizens, and those of many lesser states, think worth maintaining. That is not merely apparent, but increasingly apparent, for war not merely on common human freedom but on the elemental rights of the individual is being waged over ever-widening tracts of the globe with a savagery incompatible with the survival of any liberal civilization at all.
That tragedy has had one compensation. It has driven the custodians of this freedom into closer association in common sympathy for common protection.
Then it goes on to say:
But mutual good will alone will not make the relations between two friendly nations what they need to be "under the strenuous conditions of the modern world," and it is the merit of British and American statesmanship-the credit is due to Mr. Cordell Hull more than any other single man-that it has set itself quietly and patiently to remove obstacles to full cooperation between the two countries and negotiate agreements which, without assuming any formal political significance, shall advertise to their own citizens and to the world their resolve to substitute practical cooperation resolutely and increasingly for economic or any other form of conflict. The fundamental value of the Anglo-American trade agreement lies as much in the sacrifices each country was ready to make as in the advantages it secured for its own traders-for till it is realized that every such negotiation must be based on the simple principle of give and take the attempt of each side to concentrate on taking must spell inevitable disaster. Hardly less important were the concurrent negotiations between the United States and Canada and the treaty signed by the union and the dominion simultaneously with the major Anglo-American agreement. That, and the fact that other British
1724	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
dominions like Australia had to be brought into the discussions because concessions made to America might affect their own trade with Britain, opens up suggestive possibilities.
Then the editorial goes on to speak of the Ottawa agreements of 1932, and it has this
to say:
It to some extent decreased the trade and to a considerable extent increased the suspicions and antagonisms of states outside the empire,
articularly the United States and Germany.
ince then, and to some extent in consequence, Germany has developed a closed economy based on trade by barter, which makes the prospect of any beneficial commercial agreement with her remote. But that fact, unfortunate in itself, has had some favourable reactions, in producing the recognition among states which still prefer free interchange of the need for increasing trade among themselves. The Anglo-American agreement has gone far to meet that need, for through the operation of the most favoured nation clause it means that the tariffs of both countries are lowered not merely in relation to one another, but to all countries with which they have signed most favoured nation treaties.
It goes on to say:
In what form and by what methods the Ottawa circle can be widened, with economic consequences that would produce political results no less valuable than the economic, are matters for further thought. But Mr. Hull, Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. Stanley have performed a service of no small value in turning the minds of all reflective men in that direction.
A quotation from the Economist-and this is worthy of note-dated November 19, 1938, speaking about the trade agreement in a laudatory way, says:
All those on either side who have worked for this agreement have the right to congratulate themselves on its successful birth. And, if bouquets are being distributed, one of the largest must be reserved for Mr. Mackenzie King. Even the briefest study of the terms of the agreement is enough to show how little could have been done without the readiness of Canada to offer her generous cooperation.
It is recognized by members of the government, by the Liberal party, yes, and by the citizens of Canada, that the central and directing figure in all these negotiations was the Prime Minister of Canada. Time will tell, and history will record this as one of the finest achievements in Canada's history, and a lasting tribute to the genius of our Prime Minister.
When British empire countries were arranging trade agreements, and having especially in mind the fact that the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett insisted on Great Britain changing her fiscal policy to one of protection, when he insisted that preferences be

granted to countries of the British commonwealth by raising duties against other countries, rather than by lowering tariff barriers and other impediments to trade between empire countries, I was somewhat anxious as to the effects this would have on other nations. I still ask, what was its effect? I quoted British opinion as to its effect. In these trade agreements between Canada and the United States, and the United States and the United Kingdom, the British empire has shown its desire to trade more freely, not only with the United States, but, under the most favoured nation clause, with other countries as well; and, as I said, the Prime Minister has made it abundantly clear in his statement to the house during this debate that Canada desires to trade with all countries willing to trade with us on a fair basis. When all countries are prepared to adopt this attitude, and put it into practice, we may hope for international goodwill, and the removal of the fear of war.
Mr. Speaker, I think we have heard enough in the house during this debate to know that between parties there is a vital difference. Within a very short time we shall have an opportunity of having every party in the house record its vote as to where it stands. In this country hereafter we shall know definitely and accurately whether the Conservative party is going along the same road and in the same direction as the Liberal party. And those of us who record our vote, whether it be to-night or on another day, will have made an everlasting record as to where we stand, because in the trade agreement we have something which is beneficial not only to Canada but to the United States. We have a tripartite agreement between ourselves, the United States and Great Britain, which points the way to a solution of difficulties not only between those countries, but also among all the countries of the world.
I heartily support the resolution, and I trust that when the vote is taken we may be unanimous in declaring that we put our country ahead of our party, and that we support the agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to the resolution before the house I would suggest to hon. members opposite that their constant glorification of the trade treaty, and their constant crowing and blowing, to use a rather vulgar expression, with respect to the effects of the trade treaty, remind me very much of the old Chinese proverb which was quoted the other

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
day in the Alberta legislature, and which has been quoted on many previous occasions- "The crowing hen never lays eggs."
An hon. MEMBER-. The crowing hen?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I can assure hon. members that all the crowing they are doing about the trade treaty is not going to produce good effects, so far as Canada is concerned.
I am not commencing my address as most hon. members on the Liberal side do, namely, by suggesting that unexpectedly they were called upon to take part in the debate. Having been prepared since the resolution was introduced, I am ready to take part in the debate, but it is not my intention to do so. I recognize the futility of presenting arguments, to any great extent, in the House of Commons as it is at present constituted, and I do not care to waste my efforts. I would rather place the work I have done in analysing the effects of the treaty before an audience which will at least listen with some degree of appreciation and will give at least some weight to the facts presented to them.
I say this after due and deliberate consideration, considering the treatment I received when I attempted to address the house on Tuesday afternoon of this week. I want to say further that if the house does not raise itself above its present level, the people of Canada will themselves take steps to remedy the situation.

We have heard "order" too frequently in the house to pay very much attention to a word of that kind. Before placing on Hansard a record of what I had intended to say, I should like to make brief reference to two hon. members. I have not had an opportunity to do so before. I have great admiration for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and it is my hope and prayer that his health will continue to improve to such an extent that he may continue to grace the public life of Canada. May I also make passing reference to a friend who sits with us on this side of the house, who is at present seriously ill, and for whose recovery every hon. member is hoping. Rather than continue the debate, I am merely going to do what we sometimes do
in school. Hon. members will excuse my referring to the class-room, but that is my natural habitat. At times we ask the pupils to write essays and compositions, and at other times we ask them to develop plans along certain lines. I am going to give the house the plan which I should have elaborated considerably had I spoken earlier in the debate. I had hoped that when I got through with that elaboration I should have been able to leave this treaty so stark bare that even members on the Liberal side of the house would see the hideousness of the implications involved in it.

speechtext:
First, I was going to say
that our industries were not taken into the confidence of the government. They were not given an opportunity to submit arguments. That is quite different from the policy of the United States. I was going to refer hon. members to the United States statutes, volume forty-eight, page 943, where they would find section 4 of an act which sets out definitely the policy of the United States. That is something we have not in this country. The government- of Canada do not seem to realize the seriousness of signing a trade treaty with a foreign party. They do not seem to realize that that foreign power may be hedged in by certain definite statutes, outside which they cannot go. Those engaged in commercial enterprise, those engaged in industry in this country, and even members of parliament were not informed of what the government were doing. Yet the government come before this parliament of free people with this treaty. The whole thing seems preposterous to me. It is a far-fetched procedure. We are now debating a trade treaty which has been signed and which is in effect, and yet members of this parliament did not have a word to say as to whether that treaty should or should not be signed, as to whether the various items in the treaty were going to affect their parts of the country adversely or otherwise.
We have had one glaring example of this already in the case of cattle. When this government signed the treaty they did not know the possible results of that one item and
1720	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
they had to get an explanation. I can see the representatives of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) going hat-in-hand to the President of the United States and saying. "We are very sorry, but we did not quite understand the meaning of that particular paragraph; we thought we were going to get so many head of cattle into the United States, and instead of that you tell us it is only so many; cannot you do something for us"? The President of the United States, seeing the meekness with which he is approached, and being in a conciliatory mood, agrees to let them have a certain concession.
The same thing is true with regard to wheat. Can one imagine a more ridiculous situation than this country with its bins filled to overflowing with wheat and yet importing wheat under this trade treaty to which the Liberal members are content to agree and to which the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) hoped we would give a unanimous expression of opinion! This country, overflowing with wheat, is importing thousands of bushels to be milled.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The trade agreement does not mention wheat.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: But it is coming in; that is the difficulty.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
If the hon. member who has just spoken knew half as much as the least on this side of the house, he would be a credit as a member of parliament.
The second point I wanted to make is that I would take strong exception to the most favoured nation clause. I was going to read certain articles in the trade agreement in order to show that it is utterly impossible to make a suitable and practical trade agreement with foreign countries if we are going to embody in each and every one the most favoured nation clause. I realize that previous governments have done this. Previous governments have made mistakes, but it is up to this government to remedy such mistakes. Our bargaining powers would be much more effective if we could go to a country and bargain for reciprocal trade, knowing that that was not going to affect our trade with any other country with which we had an agreement.
I was going to go further into that argument. I was going to deal with the argument which the Prime Minister put forward in the supplementary edition of his speech on the trade treaty when he referred to the totalitarian states. I was going to take exception to his suggestion that we should and would make 
agreements with these totalitarian states as long as they maintained their present position with their dictatorial rulers and their oppression of minority races. Trade with them by all means, but do not trade with them under their present form of government and while they follow their present policy of the suppression and oppression of minority races.
As my third point I was going to read what Lord Beaverbrook had to say about this treaty. He commended it very highly from the British point of view. He pointed out what Great Britain was going to gain under the treaty signed with the United States at the same time. I was going to read what Mr. Cordell Hull had to say from the United States point of view. If we are to believe the statements of these men that Great Britain and the United States have made tremendous gains as a result of these treaties, those gains must have been made at the expense of the third party, the Dominion of Canada. If I took the time to read what Lord Beaverbrook had to say, hon. members would find that he suggests that the British dominions would have to make certain sacrifices. We are making certain sacrifices, but we do not need to make more in order to get a favourable trade agreement.	[DOT]
The fourth point I was going to elaborate was in connection with the effect of the 1935 trade treaty. I was going to quote what had been said by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) to show the house how preposterous were the statements they made in 1936 when viewed in the light of 1939. If the trade treaty of 1935 worked so disastrously for the Dominion of Canada, how can we believe them when they suggest that this treaty is going to be better than the 1935 one?
Next, I was going to refer to the effect of the agreements of 1932 on empire trade. I was going to show by means of figures that the agreements of 1932 were of tremendous value to this country, but they have been superseded more or less by this present treaty.
I was going to show that by the removal of the six cents preference on wheat we are short-circuiting our own traffic from our own Canadian ports, and I was going to ask the members from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to try to justify the loss of traffic to our eastern ports of Saint John and Halifax. If they could justify the conditions that prevailed in those ports during this winter, I would give them credit for more ingenuity than I think they possess. We are short-circuiting our traffic from our own eastern ports, and I for one am going to protest

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
most vigorously at an opportune moment, because I am interested particularly in one of our eastern ports, the port of Montreal.
The ministers of the crown do not seem to realize that there is a strong economic pull away from our eastern Canadian ports, and that we have to do something to eliminate or overcome that strong economic pull. I was going to read in support of my argument a letter addressed to the Prime Minister from Mr. W. R. Eakin, president of the Shipping Federation of Montreal, and representations from the board of trade of Montreal and from others who are interested in our Canadian ports, not only Montreal but our maritime ports and the port of Quebec.
For my sixth point I was going into the history of reciprocity and would have proved pretty conclusively that reciprocity has always been a nefarious instrument in the economic development of this country. It has always worked to the disadvantage of Canada. I was going to focus the attention of the house upon the historical development of trade treaties between Canada and the United States as they have affected this country. I was going to point out the effects of the changes made in the economic policies of the United States of America.
Some of my friends in this house will remember the wonderful trade we built up in cattle prior to 1922. The cattle of Canada passed from north to south, but in 1922 the Republican government terminated the then existing tariff in the United States, and what happened? Our cattle were stopped at the border. Our markets were glutted with cattle, and prices of beef went down to such an extent that Canadian farmers could not afford to continue in that line of business. We had to find new markets, and we found them by shipping our cattle east and west instead of north and south. Now this trade treaty comes in with a view to diverting a part of that trade.
One cannot play with trade routes the way this government is playing with them. Trade routes become firmly and definitely established, and once we have a definite trade route and are profiting by it, it is well for us to stay in that route and not to branch out of it. If we lose a good trade route we have lost something that is hard to regain, and if we are now going to sacrifice the market that we have in Great Britain at the present time, we shall have great difficulty in getting that market back again in the future. Get it back we shall have to, because if history repeats itself, and mark you, Mr. Speaker, history always does repeat itself-and always our 71492-109
trade agreements with the United States have only spelled ruin so far as Canada was concerned-this particular trade treaty will in turn be abrogated in due course, as always has happened because the policy of the United States government is not towards that kind of trade. Then we shall have to find new trade routes, and that is going to be rather difficult.
For my seventh point I was going to take a specific industry in Canada, the dress industry, and I was going to show by figures exactly what this trade treaty means to that business. What does it mean? It means the complete elimination of the dress manufacturing business in this dominion, and that means a tremendous loss to Montreal and Toronto. Bear in mind, too, that with that industry go all the allied industries associated with it, including those engaged in the manufacture of fabrics who supply the dress manufacturers with the materials wdth which to make their dresses. These goods are coming in now from the United States of America. Not only are they coming in and meeting certain restrictions by our customs, but we are actually facilitating their coming in. I know of a very large shipment of dresses that came in to the Robert Simpson Company of Toronto. They came right through to the Robert Simpson Company's store in Toronto, right up to the floor on which those dresses were to be sold, and there they were unpacked.
I was also going to show the effect of the $100 exemption on this particular trade. I was coming from New York once and there was a lady sitting opposite with three suitcases. The inspector came along and asked her, "Have you anything to declare?" She said, "yes", and he gave her a slip, upon which she wrote down so many dresses, so many hats, so many shoes, and it totalled up to probably S99.99. The inspector took the slip and looked at it and said, "Is that all you have to declare?" She replied "yes"; the inspector said, "Thank you", and that was all. He did not open her suitcases, did not look into them at all; he simply took her word and passed on. That is the way in which the $100 exemption is working so far as the dress-goods trade is concerned. I go to New York but I do not buy a suit of clothes there; but when the women go they buy dresses, hats, shoes and other apparel, and bring them back in as large quantities as the law will permit.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Is the hon. member opposed to the exemption?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I opposed it when it was first introduced. I am very, very glad that the hon. chief whip of the Liberal party is

1728	COMMONS
Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
able to resume his place in the house, because I have missed his happy questions and his occasional cross-fire, and I trust that his health will permit him to be in his seat almost continuously from now to the end of the session.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: But that does not answer my question.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I answered it. I said that I opposed the exemption when it was first introduced; I oppose it now because it works an injury to manufacturing industries established in my own city; and if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) were in his seat, I would include those in the city of Quebec as well; for there is a great shoe industry established there right in his own riding, and he also should be opposing this exemption if he had the real interests of his constituents at heart.
I am going to conclude with a suggestion. I am not finding fault with every item in this trade treaty. There are good features in any treaty; there are some good features in this one. I would have elaborated on that point if it had been my desire to do so. But I just want to leave with the house this one suggestion. It came to my mind as the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Clarke) was speaking. I was sitting beside the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) and we recalled another expression by that famous United States president. I cannot quote his exact words, but he said something like this: If you buy goods from a foreign country, you have the goods and they have your money; but if you buy goods made at home you have the goods and you have the money too.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: He never said anything of the kind.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It was Barnum who
made that statement.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Question.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few of my Liberal friends were asking for the question to be put, and put now, I suppose. But the question is not going to be put for half an hour. Some hon. members who are left in the house and who would like to go to the hockey match will find themselves remaining here if they are going to vote. The thought occurred to me as I looked round the chamber that, in so far as I wanted to say something to the ministry, perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you might page the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), the Minister of Transport (Mr. 
Howe), the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), and particularly-

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: That is small.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
-the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), who should be here guiding this bill through the house. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) asked to be excused; we will excuse him. While they are coming in, I would ask hon. members to try to think not only of this trade treaty in its own terms but also of the added effect of the treaty of 1935.
I have listened with a good deal of interest to the speeches of ministers of the crown, particularly the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and of other Liberal members.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Here he comes.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I must say that to my mind the speakers seem to have entirely ignored all the difficulties. I appreciate very much that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has come into the chamber. I was just saying to him and to his colleagues that-

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Louder.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The reason I spoke in such a high tone of voice was that I thought perhaps the minister might hear me up in his room or at the hockey match. The particular question I wish to put is this, what is this treaty going to do for the expansion of employment in Canada? What did the last treaty do to help out unemployment? Did it make for more employment?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
By the time I have finished perhaps the real situation may look a little bit different.
For twenty years it has been my pleasure to trade each and every week with my friends in the United States. Not a month goes by but I consummate a deal in Great Britain. Five cars lying in Montreal cannot go to Germany, although they are properly sold there, because of the two kinds of currency which are in vogue and because they are demanding a barter arrangement before they will permit a bona fide sale of goods to that country. For twenty years Italy has received goods which I have had the pleasure of shipping, yet this year we cannot ship there. With that background I approach this question of trade, perhaps thinking I know something about how we deal with our fellow men in these other countries.
An hon. member has said that the Conservative party could not make up their minds

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
as to what they were going to do. We studied these problems and we listened to what others in other lands were saying. 1 was particularly struck with a statement which appeared on November 26 last in the London Economist, page 485:
In these cases the effect of the agreement will largely be to divert a quantity of trade from dominion (largely Canadian) to American hands without increasing the total volume of
imports.
That is a startling statement. So I checked up on what the Prime Minister had to say when he introduced the last agreement. He said this:
The government of the United States and the government of this country were actuated by one desire, namely to make an agreement that would be equally beneficial to both countries.
Then, instead of making a statement of fact, the Prime Minister-as he is prone to do- asks a question:
Could anything destroy the agreement more effectively than that it should be shown in the course of this next three years that one country had got considerably the better of the other? Would not the effect of an agreement reached in that way be to destroy the possibility of its continuance beyond the period of three years?
Implying that if it did it would not be continued. The evidence is all against the 1935 agreement so far as that is concerned; and I call to witness the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in his budget speech of last year, wherein he said:
Total exports to the United States fell six per cent below the figure for the previous year to a total of $343,000,000, while imports at $487,300,000 showed an increase of nearly 24 per cent.
There, Mr. Speaker, is evidence from the Prime Minister's own Minister of Finance that the 1935 agreement did not work to the general advantage and benefit of Canada, and the implication should have been sufficient for the Prime Minister not to rush down to Washington to consummate another agreement at any cost, but to mark time and see whether or not one should be consummated.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce made a speech in this house a few weeks ago. Did he review the trade as from 1935 to date? Did he give us anything constructive or concrete upon which we could cast an intelligent vote in favour of this agreement? He contented himself with taking just the January, 1939, figures. In one short sentence he said: "Of course a month's figures are not sufficient".
But at the same time he had the audacity to quote them to this house.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
And he went on to say, even as the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Ivinley) said, that in January we had a great increase in exports from this country. I suppose he got his statistics from the bureau of statistics and under his own signature, in like manner as I have mine. But why did not the Minister of Trade and Commerce, why did not my friend who sits to my right here, read the line all the way through and show that for the ten months ended January 31, 1939, our exports to the United States shrank by 16-1 per cent, or $60,000,000, rather than use just the one month's figures, for January, which showed us an increase over the figure for January, 1938?
If he is going to stick to January, let us stick to the true facts, as the Prime Minister was wont to say when he was talking about the Canadian press release. Tell the people of Canada that there were no gold bullion exports in the figures for January, 1938, whereas in January of this year the government bolstered its figures by adding in $10,255,000 of gold bullion exports. I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, go a little further. He knows and I know that in December, just prior to this January month, the figures for which he put on Hansard, trade was $4,235,000 against us. He knows and I know that ever since November 16, when this trade treaty of 1938 was signed, manufacturers and anybody else shipping goods to the United States held back their shipments to get the full advantage of any concessions which were given to Canada under the Canada-United States trade agreement. He knows and I know that there were quotas in this new deal, and the rush to get the quotas in before January 31 had the effect of expanding by several million dollars our January exports.
Let us look at the other side of the picture. Importers and the like, who went to import goods from the United States are not bringing in their full spring requirements now. Why? They are holding back their imports in order to take full advantage of that three per cent excise tax ruling, the million dollars a month of excise which this treaty has given away and which comes off shortly. Watch the figures for February, March, April and May and see what happens. I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the picture which the government has put on the Canadian Hansard is not a fair picture to give to the people, if all the considerations are noted.
1730	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: When I gave the figures with regard to increased exports in January, it was in reply to what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) had stated when he said time would tell. I was showing that time had already told to the extent of one month.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Let 11s go a little further. Time will tell? Time has told already. When these negotiations were consummated at Washington, they used, as the minister knows, the figures supplied by the Department of Commerce at Washington. Take on the one hand the statistics supplied at Washington, and on the other the statistics supplied by our own bureau of statistics, and you find what the minister recited, as far as total trade is concerned, when he spoke on the address. On the other hand, taking the figures from the Department of Commerce at Washington -and those were the figures used in the negotiations-you find an adverse balance of trade against Canada for the twelve months ended December 31, 1938, amounting to $196,107,000. The minister shakes his head. Well, I will read the figures from the United States government's publication.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Which publication?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The publication issued by the Department of Commerce at Washington, dated February 7, giving the value of exports and imports for home consumption by grand divisions and countries.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Why not use the Canadian figures?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The minister used them, and I refer to them to show that he did not take the whole line. He stopped when he came to an adverse trade against us of 16-1 per cent. My hon. friends on the Liberal benches did likewise. For the twelve months ended December 31, 1938, imports by Canada from the United States for home consumption amounted to $452,852,000 while exports into the United States were $256,745,000. Take the mean of the two sets of figures, and even then I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce-I think I should call him the minister of trade for Waterloo North because he looks after only the industries in that constituency-and to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), who has just come to life and now sits behind him, that this trade balance alone means the jobs of 100,000 Canadians. If these goods could be produced in Canada in the secondary industries, 100,000 more of our people would be put to work.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Were they employed in 1932?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: That was the bottom of the world depression.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I will go back to 1932 and I will go back to the minister's Purvis commission, who folded up their tent and silently stole away and are now doing nothing about the unemployment situation. We find in this new trade agreement the very items that were in the 1935 treaty, showing that employees in the secondary industries, in two important groups, are out of employment. What item more than anything else in these two treaties has been seriously affected? Iron and steel and all the groups that fall into that category, including machinery, have been more seriously affected than any other group; and yet walking the streets of Canada to-day, according to the report, I have before me, there are 45,000 iron and steel workers who are without jobs. In paper products, printing and advertising there are 7,104. In lumber and the products of lumber, there are 7,445. Let me give some other figures:
Number out
Industry	of employment
Rubber products	 5,199
Primary coal products	 3,729
Clay, glass, stone	 5,526
Chemicals	 1,136
Electrical apparatus	 5 261
Other industries	 22,760
In other words, we have a total of 86.610; and when one takes transportation services, hotel services, trade and commerce, the retail trade and so on, we can add another 30,000. These are the people who should be employed now but are not.
Of course my hon. friends will say that I am giving only one side of the picture. Let me give them the other side. There has been some increase in employment in Canada in some branches. But will any hon. member rise in his place and say that in the textile industry, which since 1929 has had an increase in employment, that increase was not made possible by the Bennett emergency session? They know that the Bennett emergency tariffs reestablished the textile industry, and reestablished it to the extent, as the Minister of Labour is well aware, of 11,000 hands.
Under this trade treaty, by handing some of this business over to the United States, the textile industry is to-day in a precarious position. Logging as a primary industry has added 13,561 to its payroll since 1930, and the reason for that is well known. It is the same reason that caused the packing industry to add 5,000 to their payroll since that time-all as a result of the empire trade treaties. But what we gained under the

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
Bennett emergency session and in the empire trade treaties is being lost to us by the paralyzing of the secondary industries through these two agreements.
Have we really the machinery with which to make these deals? The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) mentioned Mr. Wilgress, Mr. Robertson and Mr. Hector McKinnon, three able, hardworking civil servants, three of the best we have. But are they equipped? Have they the necessary help and assistance? Are they not rather charged primarily with the responsibility for correspondence and all the business that comes to their own departmental desks? Is not Mr. Wilgress looking after commercial intelligence? Are not he and his secretary and stenographer charged with that responsibility? I have not the pleasure of knowing Mr. Robertson, but I assume he is busy with his own Department of External Affairs.
I ask you hon. members to stack up against these gentlemen the conditions obtaining in the United States on the one hand and in Great Britain on the other. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that at Washington, all the time, all the year round, there are secretariats looking after all kinds of producer organizations and all kinds of industry. He knows that as far back as January, 1938, to November, 1938, when the deal was signed, the Americans knew what goods would be affected. Their representatives were, busy. I attended a meeting in Chicago as early as April-the deal was to come off in November-and I know they were then figuring ways and means to make sure that their production would not be harmed. The cotton growers met in April; the horticultural and agricultural groups met at Washington and studied the whole plan of action; they knew exactly what they were going after. Did this government recognize the horticultural societies? Did the Minister of Agriculture recognize the grain growers' association? Did the government recognize the Canadian Manufacturers' Association? Were these people called in? Did they have a chance? Did they know what was going to happen? Did the Minister of Labour call in the Federation of Labour? Did labour know what was going to happen to them? No! "Wait until you get it and then take it and like it." That has been the policy of this administration in drawing up their trade treaties. Yet they say, " We follow the British way." .
Did they follow the British way? They did not. In London, on the Strand and up Kingsway you can go into scores of offices
where you will find organizations and associations embracing all producing and manufacturing institutions in the British isles, and each association has its own chartered accountant who has access at all times to the books of each and every industry in order to see that their interests are looked after, through the board of trade, and by the way the president of that board is an active cabinet minister in England. But they even go further than that. I do not need to remind this house that they have one highly trained body of men whose duty it is to look after trade matters in order to see that imports come into that country only under the supervision of the import duties advisory committee. Would hon. members stack up our three junior men here against such men as Right Hon. Lord May, KB.E., at $25,000 yearly; Sir Sydney J. Chapman, K.CB., C.B.E., at $15,000; Sir Allan Powell, CB.E., at $15,000; Sir Percy W. L. Ashley, K.B.E., C.B., at $10,000, and all the staff officers associated with them? They are organized to look after the interests of Great Britain in connection with matters of trade.
I ask those members of parliament who are here; I ask the ordinary member, what do you know about this trade treaty? I do not think you know a great deal about it; that is my frank, considered opinion, after listening to this and many other debates. I say that in a kindly way, because I know hon. members have a great deal to do; but I say it is not fair to Canada to charge our three commissioners with the responsibility of looking after a matter of this sort. And may I say that if any supporters of the party in power in Great Britain were to ridicule the president of the board of trade as some of our free trade friends are wont to ridicule the heads of similar organizations in Canada; or if they were to ridicule the organizations which serve that board, they would be read out of their party. Here it seems to be considered rather a fine thing to ridicule the manufacturers' association, the lumbermen's association and other similar organizations.
To sum up the whole situation, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce complains because my leader said population was not a fair basis of comparison, and said that we were a great trading country and should be considered on a par with the United States or with Great Britain in a trade deal, I say to him that the odds are fifty to one against us in regard to organization in consummating any such agreement. That is the position as it stands to-day.
1732	COMMONS
Canada-United, States Trade Agreement

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: What officials were employed by the Bennett administration when they tried to negotiate a trade treaty with the United States? Precisely the same ones that we used.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The minister reminds me
of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman); he also goes back into history. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) went back to 1842. Not satisfied with that, the hon. member for Huron North went back to Adam and Eve. Why not look ahead instead of to the rear? I like to look forward and not backward, and I want to put the facts on record. We are up against a difficult situation in trying to consummate a deal with the United States. Their mode of living, tastes and possible production are all very much the same as ours, with the result that every time we open our markets to them we have to restrict our own production. On the other hand Great Britain, which is the world's largest purchaser, is a complementary market, and that is a real advantage. It is only common sense that we must retain the preference we now possess. Sir Wilfrid Laurier believed in it; Right Hon. R. B. Bennett consummated it, but now what do we find? We find this government narrowing the preference, meddling with what we already have, to our own detriment, as is indicated in the passage I read from the London Economist. My hon. friends opposite seem to have lost their British make-up in some way or another. "What we have we hold'' seems to have been something in the past as far as they are concerned.
It is perhaps unnecessary for me to say this, but I see the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) in the house, so I might remind him that our vegetable and fruit growing conditions are not the same as they are in the United States. Their climate is so much ahead of ours that they have a natural advantage over us. It is also common knowledge that they are over-industrialized in their secondary industries, and that they are anxious to get their extra capacity operating. When they do so they will produce more than they need for themselves, and when we lower our valuations for duty purposes and the other restrictions against dumping, the result will be that millions of dollars worth of their extra production will be dumped into this country, and more of our own people will be without work.
The hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) told the house a short time ago that he opposed the $100 free entry. I do not believe in allowing S100 worth of goods to be 
brought in by tourists; I say that condition should not obtain in this country; for the reason that these goods consist of clothing, boots and shoes, dresses, refrigerators, radios, small motors and things of that kind which have a high labour content. The records show $6,000,000 of imports coming in free under that exemption, and we know there is another $6,000,000 not recorded; so, if we know anything at all about it, we know that means $1,200,000 taken from the wage rolls of the people of Canada.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Why does the hon. gentleman say there is another $6,000,000 not recorded? I ask the question for information.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: For the very simple reason that the efficiency of our customs men at border ports, as the minister knows, is only fair. When I went to school and got a mark of "fair" on an examination, it meant that I was rated at fifty or more. So I would say the efficiency is about fifty per cent, and I believe the minister will agree with me.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: No. I just wanted the basis for my hon. friend's statement.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The spirit of these trade
agreements is something that should be given more thought. Each year sees revenue bills passed by the United States against the natural products of this country. Even during 1938, sawed timber was added to the revenue bill in order that Uncle Sam might collect $1.50 a thousand feet on it. That is a new touch. But the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie)-and if he is at the hockey match I hope he can hear me-says, "Oh, but we hope that $1.50 will be taken off in June." Some hon. member to my right says there is no doubt about it, but let me remind my hon. friend that Canada has in this agreement agreed to relinquish further its guaranteed preference on lumber if and when the United States repeals the import tax on Canadian lumber. They have already sold us out in that regard, which means that more and more of the lumber we formerly sent to Great Britain under the British preference will be displaced by lumber coming from the United States. What about copper, with its four cents a pound, in all its ramifications placed against us as a revenue tax in 1934?
I should like to say something about animal oils and fats, and butter. The Liberal party are sliding down so fast on that toboggan of 40,000.000 or 50,000,000 pounds of surplus butter which is in Canada at the present time that they will hit bottom when the next election comes. Even though they

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
have had a reference before their tariff board for over two years, asking that something be done in like manner to that which was done in the United States with respect to vegetable oils and fats going into that country, to the tune of from three to six cents per pound excise tax, nothing has been done in Canada. This is another example of the do-nothing administration.
And with what other result? The result has been that imports of this substitute for our natural fats have risen from the figure of 90,000,000 pounds which was reached about five years ago, until in the year ending December 31, 1938, it reached the figure of 255,000,000 pounds. There is as much vegetable oil coming into Canada, free of all duty and tax, as there is creamery butter made in this country. Yet this administration sits impotent, and does nothing about the matter. It does not call for the tariff board report; nothing is done about it. That is another example of the revenue tax legislation of the United States-and we may expect more of it.
The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) has come into the chamber-I had not noticed him before. He had something to say this afternoon about duties, and about our exports and imports. But he seemed to have forgotten that in 1930 the United States put through their tariff act of that year with the result that our exports to that country in the year dropped by $128,000,000, or 42 per cent. So I will ask the page boy to present my hon. friend with a copy of the tariff act of 1930 of the United States, and when he has finished with it he can return it to the library of parliament.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Yes, half a dozen of them
-as long as it does not come off my time.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Does he deny the favourable
trade balance figures given this afternoon?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend deny
the unfavourable trade balance figure of $196,000.000 for the year 1938, which I gave when he was on his way home from the hockey match, a little while ago? A hundred thousand of our people are looking for jobs. The hon. member quoted figures this afternoon, but I would say to him there are only 100,000 employees in the primary industries and there are 900,000 in the secondary industries. The rate is nine to one. Put your secondary industry unemployed men to work.
I should like to say something about transportation, and cutting off the business of our
ports. I should like to say something about coal. I should like to say something about magazines and advertising which, in 1936- including magazine and other literature imports-stood at $2,900,000 and in 1939 had jumped to $5,900,000, filling this country with advertisements of all kinds of produce from the United States, and paralyzing our industry.
But the house will learn more of that anon.
I have only five minutes left. Divide up the work of the Minister of Finance with the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has taken the work on tariffs of the Minister of Finance entirely off the board for three years, because the scope of our aggregate trade shows these astounding and astonishing figures: By this agreement seventy per cent of the trade of Canada is hamstrung for three years. There is $350,000,000 worth of trade within the confines of this trade agreement-and there is nothing the government can do about it. They have extended the most favoured nation treatment affecting trade valued at $241,000,000. The margin of our preference with Great Britain has been narrowed.
I wish the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) were in his seat. I have something on my desk I should like to give to him. This is your job, Mr. Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Prime Minister stated at page 904 of Hansard-and I shall not bother looking it up; hon. members can look it up for themselves-when he was talking about trade relations with Canada, "We want to give the exact truth." That is what he said, as reported in Hansard. But he gave only a half truth when he issued that press release pamphlet, and only a half truth when he made his speech in the House of Commons. At my own expense I put a staff of university students of commerce and finance to record our trade and the effects of the 1935 treaty, and what did I find? For one reason, and one only, I did not intend to speak on the trade treaty, and that is that the treaty as such has been in operation only since January 1. All this debating which has taken place in the House of Commons with respect to the trade treaty, to a very great extent has been w'aste effort. It is not based on facts. How could it be? We have yet to see the effects of the treaty. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), who has just taken his seat, has recorded a great array of figures; in fact, we were staggered by the millions and thousands which came rolling out. At the same time he went back into 1938. 1935 and other years. The trade treaties which wrere negotiated between Great Britain and the United States and between Canada and the United States came into effect on January 1. How can any decision be based on anything but conjecture when it goes back of this year? I doubt if the figures for January and February of this year are complete, because there are always odds and ends which come up later.
I do not think the language which has emanated from the other side of the house in condemnation of this treaty is going to sway

the people of Canada one iota. They remember quite well the period from 1930 to 1935. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) sat as a member of the price spreads committee, and he must remember the evidence given of the staggering profits which were made by the textile people and other manufacturers during those tenable years. During the greatest depression Canada has ever known, many manufacturers made immense fortunes while the majority of Canadian people were in want.
I do not intend to go back of January 1, 1938, because to my mind to do that would be useless as far as any discussion of this treaty is concerned. Canada has a small population, and in the last forty years our manufacturing industry has been developed so intensely as to outstrip our growth in population. No effort has been made to find out how the products of our industries can be distributed in Canada. I think that is our main trouble as far as trade in Canada is concerned, and this disability must be overcome in some way. There are one or two ways in which it can be done. The upper house met here some time ago and had to adjourn for lack of work. The upper house of the federal parliament had an opportunity to render real service to the people of this country by staying here and going into the railway problem, not from the point of view of unification but from the point of view of making distribution more readily available to the Canadian people.

People say that there is no possibility of changing the situation as it exists at the present time, but I say that great opportunities are available to the parliament of Canada to change the system so that we may have better distribution. We can make our railways 100 per cent efficient in the distribution of the products of our factories. That would be one of the greatest helps in increasing trade in this country.
Every Conservative member, when discussing this trade treaty, has stressed its effect upon some small manufacturing concern in his own riding which was perhaps near and dear to his heart. But not one of them has spoken on the trade treaty from the point of view of the consumers who make up the greatest part of our population. Our greatest efforts should be to make available the commodities of this country to the ordinary wage-earner, the farmer and the artisan. No speaker on the other side of the house has expressed that idea. One or twro of them were

so hard put to-night that they had to refer to the fact that the customs officers on the border were not performing their duties properly. Hon. members are advancing a very poor argument when they complain of a customs officer not making a proper examination. Canada is a country of large areas, but our population is sparse. However, we have extensive railways. A cry has gone through the country which is fostering unrest and imbuing fear in the hearts of the people-the cry of the railway problem. Our railways are our greatest adjuncts to trade. Some people advocate that our railways should be amalgamated or unified, although they do not say how that is to be done. They do not realize how many people will be thrown out of employment. I maintain that trade is one of our great problems and must be for a great number of years to come, and if we bring in a population that will help consumption, naturally our home trade is going to increase. If we get enough population in this country to consume all that we produce, does anyone think we would have to look for markets outside. With the great area we have, we should be taking advantage of international loans, and now is our opportunity to get people in to consume our goods.
So far as this particular trade treaty is concerned, we know what it has done in the two months it has been in operation, and what its results will be in the future we must leave to the future to decide. We know that it will do good. Even if we did not want to enter into a trade treaty with the United States at this time, the people of this country are cognizant of the fact that the United States and Great Britain were going to negotiate a trade treaty whether or not Canada came in. In any event, our preference in the British market would have terminated in June, and we would , have lost it then anyway. Why keep harping on what has gone and on what would have been lost in any event, with no compensating results unless an agreement had been entered into? Those are the questions which the people of Canada must consider.
I say further that we should take advantage of every opportunity that offers to increase our population. It is no use our holding on to the idea that we are going to get a population purely British. We have so big an area to populate that Canada is bound to be a cosmopolitan country. If we hold off too long, when we want population we may not be able to get population commensurate with the needs of the country and under as favourable conditions as now. So far as trade is concerned, why worry about who comes in or who does not come in to increase our population? This trade treaty is signed and it is good for three years.

But I maintain that we have to go a step further and increase the ability of our population to consume the goods we produce in this country, and we cannot do that with the small population we have now. If we want to make Canada the great country that it should be and that destiny intended it to be, we must go on and on year after year increasing our consumptive capacity for all the manufactured and basic products that we produce in Canada. I say it is no use for hon. gentlemen to rise in their places and give figures, going back ten or fifteen years. That has nothing to do with the present trade agreement. It is of no earthly use to us and does not help out the situation one bit. The safest thing we can do is to leave this trade agreement to the judgment of the Canadian people. One or two manufacturing industries may be hurt, but I venture to say that the majority will not be hurt. If there are some few industries in this country suffering from an inferiority complex, which feel inferior in business ability, management and productivity to our great neighbour nation to the south, let us bring in people who will produce the goods, and not only produce them, but distribute them and sell them at a profit.

May I say to the minister that if he attempted to make a film of that kind and do justice to the scenic beauties of the different provinces, it simply could not be done in less than twelve, fourteen or fifteen thousand feet of film. that the purpose was to coordinate the film activities of the various departments.
